subject: Archaeology
title: Sumerian Schools: The First Classrooms
description: A quick, practical guide to Sumerian Schools: The First Classrooms.

hook.text: Sumerian students went to school, did homework, and complained about their teachers — we know because they wrote about it.

buildup.text: Schools called 'edubba' trained scribes. Students copied texts, practiced signs, and memorized word lists for years.

discovery.text: Thousands of student tablets survive — many with teacher corrections in red. Mistakes were marked just like today.

twist.text: A Sumerian essay titled 'Schooldays' describes a boy being caned by multiple teachers in one day. Education was brutal.

climax.text: Only a small elite attended. Most Sumerians were illiterate. Literacy was power.

punchline.text: Homework, red marks, and strict teachers. School has not changed much in 4,000 years.

quiz.question: What did the Sumerian essay 'Schooldays' describe?
options: A student's journey to become the first female scribe
A boy being caned by multiple teachers in a single day — education was harsh
A philosophical debate about the purpose of learning

details.summary: Sumerian schools called edubba, meaning tablet house, trained scribes in cuneiform writing, mathematics, and literature. Students spent years copying texts onto clay tablets, and their practice exercises — complete with teacher corrections — survive in archaeological collections today.
details.whyItMatters: The edubba is the earliest known formal education system. Student exercise tablets reveal teaching methods, curriculum, and even student complaints that feel surprisingly modern after 4,000 years.
takeaways: Edubba schools trained scribes in writing, math, and literature
Students learned by copying texts onto clay tablets for years
Practice tablets with corrections survive as archaeological evidence

faq.question: Who attended Sumerian schools?
faq.answer: Mostly sons of wealthy families — scribal training was expensive and time-consuming. Evidence for female scribes exists but is rare. Literacy was a specialized skill held by perhaps 1-2% of the population, making scribes a powerful professional class.

faq.question: What did the curriculum include?
faq.answer: Students started with basic cuneiform signs, progressed to word lists and mathematical tables, then advanced to copying literary texts and composing original documents. The curriculum could take over a decade to complete, and discipline was reportedly strict.
